title: Time and Work

references.label: GSSSB Laboratory Assistant Detailed Syllabus, Part A (Advt. 327/2025-26)

scientificNotes: General competitive-exam quantitative-aptitude topic; included to match the exam's Part A scope.
expression: Work rate = 1 / (Time to complete alone)    Combined rate = sum of individual rates    Time together = 1 / (Combined rate)
explanation: The standard technique treats the WHOLE job as '1 unit of work'; a person/machine that completes the job alone in T days has a work RATE of 1/T (job per day). When multiple agents work TOGETHER, their rates simply ADD (assuming they don't interfere with each other) — the combined time to finish is the reciprocal of the summed rate. For a 'PIPES AND CISTERNS' variant where one pipe fills and another drains, the draining pipe's rate is subtracted (treated as negative) rather than added. The same logic extends to 'man-days' problems: total work = (number of workers) × (number of days) × (rate per worker per day), which stays constant for a fixed job — letting you solve for any one unknown (workers, days, or efficiency) given the other two are changed.

variables.meaning: Time taken by one person/machine to complete the job alone
Fraction of the job completed per unit time
Sum of all individual rates (net, if some are draining/opposing)

workedExample.scenario: A can complete a job in 12 days, B in 18 days. Working together, how long will they take?

commonMistakes: Averaging the two individual TIMES directly (e.g. (12+18)/2) instead of combining their RATES — time doesn't average this way; only rates (1/T) add linearly for simultaneous work.
Forgetting to subtract (not add) the rate of a pipe/agent working AGAINST the others (e.g. an outlet pipe draining a tank while inlet pipes fill it).
genZNote: Time and work problems are just 'convert everyone to a rate, add the rates, flip it back to time' — never average the raw days directly.
